Hi everyone,

I’m trying to create a material that will keep the texture at a constant predefined size while repeating it. Often used in the prototyping phase, and very helpful to get a visual reference of the surrounding scale.

Here is preview and a [working demo](https://jsfiddle.net/j1pe9kxy/1/).

[![GridBoxPrototypeMaterial](https://canada1.discourse-cdn.com/flex035/uploads/threejs/optimized/3X/2/6/26d873293958b7ba1a3127fd306676a3320bf6b4_2_690x245.png)\\
GridBoxPrototypeMaterial900×320 117 KB](https://canada1.discourse-cdn.com/flex035/uploads/threejs/original/3X/2/6/26d873293958b7ba1a3127fd306676a3320bf6b4.png "GridBoxPrototypeMaterial")

GLSL is not my forte, so i’m cheating on the texture generation part, using a 2D canvas, while facing some problems with the GLSL part:

1. The texture is inverted on the X axis with the following cube faces:

- Positive X
- Positive Y
- Negative Z

2. The texture is centered. Not sure if it’s possible, but ideally it should stick to the corners.

3. Nothing serious, but aliasing is also an issue.


Thanks!

For issue №3 use these:

```javascript
texture.minFilter = THREE.LinearMipmapLinearFilter;
texture.anisotropy = 16;
```

Note, that it is not good to use constants like 16, it is better to use **renderer.getMaxAnisotropy()**. In the code the texture is created before the renderer, that’s why I did not use the renderer to get the maximal anisotropy.

Upgraded!

Now instead of using `ShaderMaterial`, I’m extending the material with `material.onBeforeCompile`. meaning it can be used with any materials.

```javascript
const material = new THREE.MeshPhysicalMaterial({
  metalness: 0.3,
  roughness: 0.3,
  transmission: 1,
});

extendToGridPrototypeMaterial(material);
```

This allow it to inherit the base material characteristics, lights, shadow, environment…

Here is the [new demo](https://jsfiddle.net/zpfd1cws/2/).

## post by Fennec on Feb 14, 2024

[![](https://yyz1.discourse-cdn.com/flex035/user_avatar/discourse.threejs.org/fennec/48/59265_2.png)](https://discourse.threejs.org/u/fennec)

[Fennec](https://discourse.threejs.org/u/fennec)

[Feb 2024](https://discourse.threejs.org/t/procedural-prototype-grid-shader/60979/12 "Post date")

It should be possible, here is the part where I’m overriding the `map` texture:

```javascript
shader.fragmentShader = shader.fragmentShader.replace(
      '#include <map_fragment>',
      `
      #ifdef USE_MAP
        vec4 sampledDiffuseColor = texture2D( map, vGridUv );
        #ifdef DECODE_VIDEO_TEXTURE
          sampledDiffuseColor = vec4( mix( pow( sampledDiffuseColor.rgb * 0.9478672986 + vec3( 0.0521327014 ), vec3( 2.4 ) ), sampledDiffuseColor.rgb * 0.0773993808, vec3( lessThanEqual( sampledDiffuseColor.rgb, vec3( 0.04045 ) ) ) ), sampledDiffuseColor.w );

        #endif
        diffuseColor *= sampledDiffuseColor;
      #endif
      `
    );
```

This particular line:

```javascript
vec4 sampledDiffuseColor = texture2D( map, vGridUv );
```

The same approach can be done to override other mappings. Find the `#include <*-fragment>` and replace it.

[![](https://yyz1.discourse-cdn.com/flex035/user_avatar/discourse.threejs.org/fennec/48/59265_2.png)](https://discourse.threejs.org/u/fennec)

This did the trick:

```javascript
shader.fragmentShader = shader.fragmentShader.replace(
      '#include <alphamap_fragment>',
      `
      #ifdef USE_ALPHAMAP
        diffuseColor.a *= texture2D( alphaMap, vGridUv ).g;
      #endif
      `
    );
```

You can see it implemented [here](https://jsfiddle.net/Lzdqhf3a/1/).

There are classes such as THREE.CubeGeometry, THREE.SphereGeometry, etc. that automatically generate the UV coordinates for you. However, if you are creating your own geometry from scratch (i.e., specifying vertex locations, creating faces, etc.) then the answer is no. Either you need to set the UV coordinates manually when creating the geometry, or you need to write a custom shader which determines the UV coordinates for any given point. Think about it this way: if you don't specify UV coordinates, the points on your geometry have no idea which point on your texture they should display.

Sure thing, Pavel! So I exported a bunch of variations, and I tried to name the files based on the parameters of the polygon.

A couple of things to keep in mind:

- There’s still a bit of work to be done on optimizing the vertex count, I used [mergeVertices()](https://threejs.org/docs/index.html?q=Buffe#examples/en/utils/BufferGeometryUtils.mergeVertices), but Blender still shows me that there are vertices that can be merged by distance.


[![Screenshot 2025-03-11 at 3.04.28 PM](https://canada1.discourse-cdn.com/flex035/uploads/threejs/optimized/3X/6/a/6a357683c125d5c0ea7674595afee179cd9ef8e7_2_353x375.jpeg)\\
Screenshot 2025-03-11 at 3.04.28 PM1920×2034 168 KB](https://canada1.discourse-cdn.com/flex035/uploads/threejs/original/3X/6/a/6a357683c125d5c0ea7674595afee179cd9ef8e7.jpeg "Screenshot 2025-03-11 at 3.04.28 PM")

- I’ve been experimenting with subdividing the path after the rounding procedure (via bezier curves).
- The API I made have 2 rounding modes (circular & natural), with 2 additional modes that still yield unreliable geometry (supershape & hand-drawn).

Let me know your thoughts!

This experiment started on d3.js, doing exactly the same thing but with SVG & Canvas, and I tried to make it in a way that the same parameters can be used to use it with Three.js.

The library [3d-assets](https://github.com/boytchev/3d-assets/blob/44a274c3624b3600926ee1e4cd98e5081c54e8bd/src/assets-utils.js#L68), that you’ve made really help me understand how to construct geometry procedurally, but what I did is not as general purpose. Regardless, thank you so much!

Let me know your thoughts!

> UV\_Grid\_Sm.jpg is actually wrong
>
> (0,0) is located bottom left not top left.

Actually, I would not say that.

three.js does not impose a particular uv convention. Note that by the GLTF convention, uv (0, 0) is located in the upper-left, and `GLTFLoader` works just fine.

three.js just expects uv (0, 0) to be located at the start of the texture buffer. `Texture.flipY` can be used to control that.

The "correct" UV reference map is one that is consistent with your geometry.

Maybe we should have two example uv reference textures: `uv_grid_opengl` and `uv_grid_directx`. There are plenty online, if you can find one that is royalty-free.
